content: Alcohol misuse among young people is a significant concern for various stakeholders, including healthcare providers, policymakers, prevention specialists, criminal justice professionals, youth workers, educators, and parents. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the effectiveness of universal multi-component prevention programs in reducing alcohol misuse among school-aged children up to 18 years old. It also sought to update findings from a previously published Cochrane systematic review. The review included evidence from studies conducted up to 2002, as identified in the earlier Cochrane review, and additional studies published through July 2010. Databases such as MEDLINE, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, EMBASE, Project CORK, and PsycINFO were searched to identify relevant studies. The inclusion criteria required randomized trials that evaluated universal multi-component prevention programs, which involved interventions delivered in more than one setting, and reported alcohol use outcomes in individuals aged 18 years or younger. Two reviewers independently screened the titles, abstracts, and full texts of the identified studies. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers using a predefined extraction form. The risk of bias in the included studies was also assessed. A total of 20 parallel-group trials were included in the review. However, the overall quality of reporting in these trials was poor. Only 25% of the trials adequately described their methods of randomization, and only 5% provided sufficient details on allocation concealment. Approximately half of the trials adequately addressed incomplete data, while this information was unclear in about 20% of the studies. Due to significant heterogeneity in the interventions, populations, and outcomes across the included trials, the results were summarized qualitatively rather than quantitatively. Out of the 20 trials, 12 demonstrated some evidence of effectiveness in reducing alcohol misuse compared to a control or alternative intervention group. The duration of these effects ranged from 3 months to 3 years. Among the remaining 8 trials, one reported significant effects using one-tailed statistical tests, while the other 7 found no significant effects of the multi-component interventions. The review also assessed whether multi-component interventions (delivered in more than one setting) provided additional benefits compared to single-component interventions. This analysis was possible in 7 trials with multiple arms. However, only one of these trials clearly demonstrated a benefit of multi-setting interventions over single-setting interventions. In conclusion, there is some evidence to suggest that universal multi-component prevention programs can be effective in reducing alcohol misuse among young people. However, there is limited evidence to support the notion that interventions with multiple components are more effective than those with single components.
